Battle of Cannae. Near the town of Cannae in southern Italy during the Second Punic War, Hannibal Barca of Carthage achieved one of history's most brilliant tactical victories, annihilating a Roman army nearly twice the size of his own. The battle on that day in 216 BC would become the most catastrophic Roman military defeat in history.

Hannibal commanded approximately 50,000 troops, while the Romans fielded roughly 80,000 soldiers under consuls Varro and Paullus. The Carthaginian general was outnumbered, but this was precisely his plan. He formed a crescent-shaped center, deliberately making it weak to draw the Roman reserves forward.

As the Roman center pressed ahead, believing victory was near, Hannibal's flanks wheeled inward. Then they closed from behind, catching the entire Roman army in a complete encirclement. The Roman soldiers were trapped with nowhere to go, unable to maneuver, unable to flee. They were slaughtered where they stood.

Estimates suggest 50,000 to 70,000 Romans were killed or captured that day. Hannibal's forces, by contrast, suffered only around 6,000 casualties. The kill ratio was roughly eight to one.

Yet despite this masterpiece of tactics, Hannibal could not translate it into lasting victory. He could not capture Rome itself, and Rome's vast resources and unshakeable will to continue fighting proved impossible to overcome. Rome eventually prevailed through superior numbers and determination. Hannibal's genius is forever linked to Scipio Africanus, who ultimately defeated him at Zama, and to the Second Punic War itself, which Cannae nearly decided in Carthage's favor.
